note: Parentheses added around two clauses the source sets off without them.
replacement: After the rout, the Corinthians did not bother to lash fast and tow away the hulls of the vessels they had disabled. Instead they turned on the men, whom they butchered as they sailed through, caring less to take prisoners. They even killed some of their own friends by mistake, not knowing that their right wing had been defeated. For the number of ships on both sides, and the distance over which they covered the sea, made it hard, once the fleets had joined, to tell conquerors from conquered. This battle proved far greater than any before it, at least any between Hellenes, in the number of vessels engaged. After the Corinthians had chased the Corcyraeans to land, they turned to the wrecks and their dead. They succeeded in getting hold of most of these and conveying them to Sybota, the meeting place of the land forces supplied by their barbarian allies. Sybota, it must be said, is a desert harbor of Thesprotis. When this task was over, they mustered again and sailed against the Corcyraeans. The Corcyraeans advanced to meet them with all the ships they had left that were fit for service, accompanied by the Athenian vessels, for they feared that the Corinthians might attempt a landing in their territory. It was by now getting late, and the paean had been sung for the attack, when the Corinthians suddenly began to back water. They had seen twenty Athenian ships sailing up. The Athenians had sent these out afterward to reinforce the ten, fearing, as it turned out justly, that the Corcyraeans would be defeated and that their handful of ships could not protect them. The Corinthians saw these ships first. They suspected that they were from Athens and that those they saw were not all, but that more were behind. So they began to retire. The Corcyraeans had not sighted the ships, since they were advancing from a point where they could not see so well. They were wondering why the Corinthians were backing water when some caught sight of the Athenians and cried out that there were ships in view ahead. At this they also retired, for it was now getting dark, and the Corinthian retreat had suspended the fighting. So the two sides parted, and the battle ceased with night. The Corcyraeans were in their camp at Leukimme when these twenty ships from Athens, under the command of Glaucon, son of Leagrus, and Andocides, son of Leogoras, made their way through the corpses and wrecks and sailed up to the camp, not long after they had been sighted. It was now night, and the Corcyraeans feared that they might be hostile vessels. But they soon recognized them, and the ships came to anchor.

note: "and also a wind" reads as the Corcyraeans picking up a wind; the wind is a cause of the scattering.
replacement: On receiving this answer from the Athenians, the Corinthians began preparing for their voyage home, and set up a trophy at Sybota, on the continent. The Corcyraeans, for their part, picked up the wrecks and dead that the current, and a wind that rose in the night, had scattered in all directions and carried out to them, and as victors they set up their own trophy at Sybota, on the island. Each side had its own reasons for claiming the victory. The Corinthians had been victorious in the sea-fight until night. This had enabled them to carry off most of the wrecks and dead, and they held no fewer than a thousand prisoners of war, and had sunk close upon seventy vessels. The Corcyraeans had destroyed about thirty ships, and after the Athenians arrived they had picked up the wrecks and dead on their own side. They had also seen the Corinthians retire before them, backing water at the sight of the Athenian vessels, and, once the Athenians had come, refuse to sail out against them from Sybota. So both sides claimed the victory.

note: Source leaves the Chalcidians and allies outside the isthmus and only the cavalry in Olynthus; candidate puts all at Olynthus.
replacement: Meanwhile the Potidæans and the Peloponnesians with Aristeus were encamped on the isthmus, on the side facing Olynthus, waiting for the Athenians, and they had set up their market outside the city. The allies had chosen Aristeus general of all the infantry, and the command of the cavalry was given to Perdiccas. He had at once left the alliance of the Athenians and gone back to that of the Potidæans, and had appointed Iolaus as his general. The plan of Aristeus was to keep his own force on the isthmus and await the Athenian attack. The Chalcidians and the allies were to stay outside the isthmus, and the two hundred cavalry of Perdiccas at Olynthus, to act on the Athenian rear when the Athenians advanced against him, so that the enemy would be placed between two fires. Meanwhile Callias the Athenian general and his colleagues sent the Macedonian horse and a few of the allies to Olynthus, to prevent any movement from that quarter. The Athenians themselves broke up their camp and marched against Potidæa. When they reached the isthmus and saw the enemy preparing for battle, they formed against him, and soon afterward the two sides engaged. The wing of Aristeus, with the Corinthians and other picked troops around him, routed the wing opposed to it and followed it a considerable distance in pursuit. But the rest of the army of the Potidæans and Peloponnesians was defeated by the Athenians and took refuge inside the fortifications. When Aristeus returned from the pursuit, he saw that the rest of the army was defeated. He was at a loss which of two risks to choose, whether to go to Olynthus or to Potidæa. In the end he decided to draw his men into as small a space as possible and force his way into Potidæa at a run. Not without difficulty, through a storm of missiles, he passed along the breakwater through the sea, and brought off most of his men safe, though a few were lost. Meanwhile the auxiliaries of the Potidæans from Olynthus, which is about seven miles off and in sight of Potidæa, had advanced a little way to help when the battle began and the signals were raised, and the Macedonian horse had formed against them to prevent it. But victory soon declared for the Athenians and the signals were taken down, and the auxiliaries retired back within the wall, while the Macedonians returned to the Athenians. So there were no cavalry present on either side. After the battle the Athenians set up a trophy and gave back their dead to the Potidæans under truce. The Potidæans and their allies had close upon three hundred killed; the Athenians had a hundred and fifty of their own citizens killed, and Callias their general.
